raw_case_text:
A 61-year-old female who had never smoked was referred to Osaka University Hospital with a productive cough, shortness of breath, and wheezing for 5 years. She had a high eosinophil range of 6-20% (normal, 2-4%) and transient recurrent infiltrates on serial chest X-rays. Eosinophilic pneumonia with bronchial asthma had been diagnosed and treatment with oral prednisolone resulted in the remission of symptoms for 2-3 weeks at a time.
The patient complained of up to 10 mL of sputum per day which was purulent, malodorous and sometimes formed mucoid plugs. She was prescribed with inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-agonists. She was found to have bilateral coarse crepitations with biphasic polyphonic rhonchi on pulmonary examination. Blood cell analysis revealed a total leukocyte count of 7240 cells/muL; with 44.7% polymorphs, 36.8% lymphocytes, 5.5% monocytes, 11.9% eosinophils, and 1.1% basophils. The absolute eosinophil count was elevated at 861/muL. Serum biochemistry findings were unremarkable, and Aspergillus spp. IgG antibody was negative. Total IgE was within the normal range (70.36 IU/mL), but specific IgE for Aspergillus spp. was found to be positive.
A chest X-ray showed infiltrates in the right lower lung (Fig. 1A), and computed tomography revealed bilateral dilation of the central bronchi in the right upper lobe (Fig. 1B). The involved bronchi contained hyperattenuating mucus. Bilateral central bronchiectasis was diagnosed. The patient was further investigated because saccular bronchiectasis is a feature of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). Direct analysis of sputum samples using random sequencing (shotgun sequence) using a next-generation sequencer revealed fungal DNA. Aspergillus fumigatus was dominant and four other fungal sequences including Schizophyllum commune were found (Table 1).
Microscopic assessment of sputum was negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) and other bacteria. However, Charcot-Leyden crystals that are generated through the breakdown of eosinophils and hyphae were identified (Fig. 1C and D). Direct microscopy of KOH wet mounts of three consecutive sputum specimens and expectorated sputum/mucoid plugs revealed two types of septate and branching hyphae (Fig. 2A and B). Homogenized sputum and mucoid plugs inoculated onto Sabouraud's glucose agar (SGA) developed green and white colonies with a wooly texture after 4 days at 2  C (Fig. 2C and D).
One of the fungi was morphologically identified as A. fumigatus (Fig. 2A and C), but the other (Fig. 2B and D) remained obscure. Therefore, DNA was extracted and the internal transcribed spacer region (ITS) and the D1/D2 region of large subunit rRNA gene were amplified by PCR. Direct sequencing of the PCR products showed that the sequences of the ITS and D1/D2 regions were 100% similar to those of various S. commune strains, such as IFM 46097. The diagnosis of allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM) due to co-infection with A. fumigatus and S. commune was made.
The susceptibility of the isolated A. fumigatus and S. commune strains to antifungal drugs (minimum inhibitory concentration; MIC) was as follows: amphotericin B (1 and 0.5 mug/mL), 5-fluorocytosine (64 and 0.25 mug/mL), fluconazole (>64 and 4 mug/mL), itraconazole (0.12 and 0.25 mug/mL), voriconazole (0.5 and 0.12 mug/mL), and micofungin (0.03 and >16 mug/mL), respectively.
The administration of oral itraconazole and prednisolone, improved the symptoms in this patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 61-year-old never-smoking female presented with a 5-year history of productive cough with malodorous mucoid plugs, shortness of breath, and wheezing.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 5 years, the patient experienced chronic productive cough (expectorating up to 10 mL/day of purulent, malodorous sputum with mucoid plugs), dyspnea, wheezing, peripheral eosinophilia (6%-20%), and recurrent transient pulmonary infiltrates that remitted for only 2-3 weeks at a time after courses of oral prednisolone alongside maintenance inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta-agonists.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed previously with bronchial asthma and eosinophilic pneumonia; lifetime non-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic productive cough with malodorous mucoid plugs, wheezing, and dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Pulmonary auscultation revealed bilateral coarse crepitations and biphasic polyphonic rhonchi.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed WBC 7,240/uL with eosinophilia (11.9% eosinophils, absolute eosinophil count 861/uL; historical range 6%-20%), 44.7% neutrophils, 36.8% lymphocytes, 5.5% monocytes, and 1.1% basophils. Serum biochemistry was normal, total serum IgE was normal (70.36 IU/mL), serum Aspergillus IgG antibody was negative, and Aspergillus-specific IgE was positive. Chest X-ray showed right lower lung infiltrates. Sputum AFB and bacterial smears were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated bilateral central saccular bronchiectasis (predominantly in the right upper lobe) impacted with high-attenuation mucus. Sputum microscopy (including KOH wet mounts of three consecutive sputum/mucoid plug samples) revealed abundant Charcot-Leyden crystals and two distinct morphologies of branching septate fungal hyphae. Shotgun metagenomic next-generation sequencing of sputum detected dominant Aspergillus fumigatus DNA alongside four other fungi including Schizophyllum commune. Culture of homogenized sputum and mucoid plugs on Sabouraud glucose agar grew green colonies morphologically identified as Aspergillus fumigatus and white woolly colonies identified by ITS and D1/D2 large-subunit rRNA PCR sequencing (100% identity) as Schizophyllum commune. Antifungal MICs (A. fumigatus / S. commune, in ug/mL) were: itraconazole (0.12 / 0.25), voriconazole (0.5 / 0.12), amphotericin B (1 / 0.5), 5-FC (64 / 0.25), fluconazole (>64 / 4), and micafungin (0.03 / >16).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM) with central bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction caused by dual fungal co-infection with Aspergillus fumigatus and Schizophyllum commune, confirmed by positive Aspergillus-specific IgE, Charcot-Leyden crystals and dimorphic septate hyphae in mucoid plugs, shotgun sputum sequencing, fungal culture, and ITS/D1/D2 rRNA PCR sequencing. Treated with combination oral itraconazole and oral prednisolone, resulting in marked clinical symptom improvement.
